name: Nāgārjuna
summary: Founder of the Madhyamaka: author of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and the other 'reasoning' treatises, of letters to a Sātavāhana king and of hymns, revered in every Mahāyāna tradition as the 'second Buddha' who opened the Perfection of Wisdom teaching of emptiness.
notes: U43 contribution: first of the seven masters of Jōdo Shinshū; the 'chapter on easy practice' of the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā (T1521 ch. 9) is the Indian root of the easy path (tea:dasabhumika-vibhasa:41b02-06).

name: Vasubandhu
summary: Author of the Abhidharmakośa and its bhāṣya, the classic summary of Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika Abhidharma with Sautrāntika criticisms; in its ninth chapter he refutes the Vātsīputrīya person and the non-Buddhist self. (This unit contributes the Abhidharma side; the Yogācāra works belong to U41.)
notes: U43 contribution: known in East Asian Pure Land as Tianqin 天親 / Seshin 世親; the Rebirth Treatise (T1524) is attributed to him; second of the seven masters of Jōdo Shinshū.

name: Bodhiruci (6th c.)
summary: North Indian monk in Luoyang (arrived 508) who translated the ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra, the Vajracchedikā, Vasubandhu's Daśabhūmika commentary and the Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa.
notes: U43 contribution: translator of the Rebirth Treatise; in the tradition's account (Xu gaoseng zhuan; Shōshinge) he gave Tanluan the Contemplation Sūtra, telling him that no Daoist longevity compares with the Buddha's immeasurable life, whereupon Tanluan burned his Daoist scriptures.

name: Kumārajīva
summary: The great Kuchean translator (344–413 or 350–409). This unit records his translations of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya and of the Satyasiddhiśāstra; his Madhyamaka and Mahāyāna work belongs to other units.
notes: U43 contribution: translator of the Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha (T366) and the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā (T1521); answered Huiyuan's questions on the pratyutpanna samādhi.

name: Amitābha / Amitāyus
alt_names: Jin jippō mugekō nyorai 尽十方無碍光如来
summary: The buddha of Immeasurable Light and Life who presides over Sukhāvatī in the west; as the monk Dharmākara he made the vows (48 in T360) to receive all who call on him.
notes: U43 contribution: in the Sanskrit Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha (GRETIL, Fujita) the vows number 47; Tanluan praises twelve names of his light; Shinran calls him the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light filling the ten directions; to Ryōnin he is said to have revealed the interfusing nenbutsu (1117).

name: Mahāsthāmaprāpta
summary: The bodhisattva of great strength, attendant of Amitābha with Avalokiteśvara; object of the eleventh contemplation of the Contemplation Sūtra; in the Śūraṅgama his penetration is by recollection of the Buddha.
notes: U43 contribution: Hōnen was regarded in his circle as a manifestation of Seishi (Eshinni's dream); Shinran composed hymns on Seishi's penetration through recollection.

name: Vaidehī
summary: Queen of Magadha, mother of Ajātaśatru, whose plea for a land without sorrow occasions the Contemplation Sūtra.
notes: U43 contribution: the sūtra calls her an ordinary being (fanfu) of feeble mind (T365 341c23); Shandao reads her as the model of the ordinary person for whom the sūtra was taught; at the end she attains the acceptance of non-arising (T365 346a27-b01).

name: Kuiji
summary: Xuanzang's principal disciple and systematizer of Faxiang, counted its first patriarch; author of the great commentaries on the Cheng weishi lun and the Nyāyapraveśa and champion of the five-gotra doctrine.

name: Saichō
summary: Founder of Japanese Tendai (767-822), who defended the Lotus's one vehicle and universal buddha-nature against Tokuitsu.

name: Huiyuan of Lushan

realization_account.text: Over his thirty years on Lushan he saw the sage forms three times in the first eleven years without speaking of it; at the end, rising from samādhi, he saw Amitābha filling space with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and was told he would be born in seven days (Fozu tongji 26).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Disciple of Dao'an who settled on Lushan (Donglin si) and never again crossed the Tiger Stream; in 402 he and 123 companions vowed together before an image of Amitābha to be born in the West (Gaoseng zhuan). He practised the samādhi of recollecting the Buddha (pratyutpanna), corresponded with Kumārajīva on it, defended the monastic order's independence from the throne, and was made the first patriarch of the Lotus school by Song writers. The 'White Lotus Society' and its 'eighteen worthies' are later names and legends (scholarly account).

name: Liu Yimin
summary: Lay scholar of Pengcheng who joined Huiyuan on Lushan and wrote the text of the vow of 402 made by 123 persons before the image of Amitābha (Gaoseng zhuan).

name: Dao'an
summary: Leading Chinese monk of the 4th c., cataloguer and organiser of monastic rules, teacher of Huiyuan; he himself vowed to be born in Maitreya's Tuṣita heaven.

name: Tanluan

scholarly.text: c. 476–c. 542 (some sources place his death after 554)

realization_account.text: After falling ill while commenting on the Mahāsaṃnipāta he sought Daoist longevity; meeting Bodhiruci in Luoyang he was given the Contemplation Sūtra, burned his Daoist texts and devoted himself to the Pure Land (Xu gaoseng zhuan; Shōshinge).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Northern Wei master trained in the Four Treatises (Sanlun) who wrote the Commentary on Vasubandhu's Rebirth Treatise, the first systematic Pure Land theology: the easy path is to be born by the power of Amitābha's vow (other-power); birth there is the 'birth of non-birth'; ten continuous recitations outweigh heavy karma; merit is transferred for going and returning. Third of the seven Shinshū masters.

name: Daochuo

realization_account.text: Tradition says that at Xuanzhong si, reading the inscription on Tanluan's deeds (609), he turned to the Pure Land at forty-eight, lectured on the Contemplation Sūtra some two hundred times and recited the name 70,000 times a day, counting with beans (Xu gaoseng zhuan; later accounts).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Master who in the Anle ji taught that in the last age of the Dharma the holy path can hardly be realised and only the Pure Land gate is passable; that Amitābha is a reward-body buddha; that ten continuous recitations suffice even for evil-doers. Popularised counting recitations (with beans or a rosary). Fourth of the seven Shinshū masters.
notes: Counting details (70,000; beans) are from biographies and recalled, low-moderate confidence.

name: Shandao
alt_names: Guangming heshang 光明和尚 / Guangming fashi

realization_account.text: Each time he recited, a ray of light issued from his mouth (Fozu tongji 26); Jōdo-shū regards him as a manifestation of Amitābha, and Hōnen dreamt of meeting him with a half-golden body.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Disciple of Daochuo who taught in Chang'an for some thirty years, copied the Amitābha Sūtra in tens of thousands of copies and painted hundreds of transformation tableaux. In his commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra he made calling Amitābha's name the rightly determined act, set out the three minds and the two kinds of deep entrusting, the five right practices, the parable of the two rivers and the white path, and held that ordinary beings are born into a reward land. The Xu gaoseng zhuan tells that a man who asked him about birth leapt from a willow tree; the Song Fozu tongji tells the same of Shandao himself (the tradition's accounts differ). Fifth Shinshū master; Hōnen 'relied solely on Shandao'.

name: Huaigan

realization_account.text: A Faxiang scholar who doubted the nianfo; on Shandao's advice he practised for three years before attaining the samādhi and seeing the Buddha's golden form (Song gaoseng zhuan, as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Disciple of Shandao and author of the Shi jingtu qunyi lun, answering Yogācāra objections to Pure Land doctrine and recommending loud recitation.

name: Jiacai
summary: Tang monk of the Hongfa si in Chang'an who systematised Daochuo's teaching in his Jingtu lun, including biographies of those born.

name: Chengyuan
summary: Ascetic Pure Land teacher of Nanyue ('the pratyutpanna master of Nanyue'), teacher of Fazhao; third patriarch in the Fozu tongji list.

name: Fazhao

realization_account.text: Tradition tells of visions of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra on Wutai who told him that recollecting the Buddha is the supreme practice (as recalled from later biographies).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Creator of the five-tone (wuhui) chanting of the name, taught at court in Chang'an; the Zhulin si on Wutai is associated with him; fourth patriarch in both Song lists. Ennin brought his chant to Mt Hiei.

name: Shaokang
alt_names: Hou Shandao 後善導 (the later Shandao)

realization_account.text: On reading a text of Shandao the image emitted light and he resolved on the Pure Land; when he recited, buddhas were seen issuing from his mouth (Song biographies, as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tang master of Muzhou (Zhejiang) called 'the later Shandao', who taught children to recite by paying them a coin per recitation and led large recitation assemblies; fifth patriarch in the Fozu tongji list.
notes: The coin episode is widely told; recalled, moderate.

name: Feixi
summary: Tang monk of the Caotang si (Zige shan), author of the Treatise on the Jewel-King Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha.

name: Cimin Huiri

realization_account.text: After travelling to India he prayed at Gandhāra and received a vision of Avalokiteśvara urging him to the Pure Land (as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tang pilgrim to India (702–719) who on his return taught Pure Land practice joined with precepts and study and criticised Chan teachers who rejected recitation as mere form.

name: Jingying Huiyuan
summary: Sui scholar-monk (not the Huiyuan of Lushan) whose commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra ranked the nine grades by the attainments of sages and ordinary beings; Shandao's commentary argues against this reading.

name: Yongming Yanshou

realization_account.text: Tradition says he drew lots before an image, choosing between meditation and the myriad good practices, and drew the latter seven times; he recited the name 100,000 times daily (Song biographies, as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Fayan Chan master of Hangzhou whose Wanshan tonggui ji defends recitation and all good practices alongside Chan; counted the sixth Pure Land patriarch in the Fozu tongji. The 'four alternatives' on Chan and Pure Land ('with Chan and with Pure Land, like a tiger with horns') are traditionally ascribed to him but are not found in the Wanshan tonggui ji (checked locally) and appear only in later sources.

name: Shengchang
summary: Song monk of Hangzhou who formed the Jingxing she (Society of Pure Conduct) of officials and monks modelled on Huiyuan's, writing out the Huayan chapter on pure conduct in his blood; last of the seven patriarchs in the Fozu tongji and fourth successor in the Lebang wenlei.

name: Ciyun Zunshi
summary: Song Tiantai master who composed Pure Land repentance liturgies and the widely used 'ten recitations' method for lay people each morning.

name: Changlu Zongze
summary: Song Chan master, compiler of the Chanyuan qinggui (1103), who founded a Lotus assembly (Lianhua shenghui) for recitation; fifth successor of Huiyuan in Zongxiao's list. His simile of farming and banking for Chan and Pure Land is cited in the Lushan lianzong baojian preface.

name: Wang Rixiu
summary: Song lay scholar of Longshu who abandoned an official career for recitation, compiled a collated edition of the Larger Sūtra (T364) and wrote the popular Longshu jingtu wen; said to have died standing while reciting.

name: Zongxiao
summary: Southern Song Tiantai monk who compiled the Lebang wenlei (1200), the first to name a line of Lotus-school patriarchs.

name: Zhipan
summary: Southern Song Tiantai historian whose Fozu tongji lists seven patriarchs of the Lotus society.

name: Huijiao
summary: Liang-dynasty monk, compiler of the Biographies of Eminent Monks (Gaoseng zhuan).

name: Jiezhu
summary: Northern Song monk who compiled the Jingtu wangsheng zhuan.

name: Mao Ziyuan

realization_account.text: In samādhi he awakened on hearing a crow's call (Lushan lianzong baojian).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Song monk of Kunshan, trained in Tiantai calming and contemplation, who founded lay repentance halls (Lianzong chantang) teaching the five precepts confirmed by five recitations of Amitābha's name and the 'perfect interfusion of the four lands'; summoned by the retired emperor in 1166 and given the title Cizhao zongzhu (Lushan lianzong baojian).

name: Pudu of Lushan
summary: Yuan monk of Donglin si on Lushan who compiled the Lushan lianzong baojian (1305) to defend the Lotus school and Mao Ziyuan against heterodox White Lotus groups.

name: Tianru Weize
summary: Yuan Linji master, disciple of Zhongfeng Mingben, whose Jingtu huowen persuades Chan practitioners to recite Amitābha's name.

name: Miaoye
summary: Ming monk who compiled the Baowang sanmei nianfo zhizhi.

name: Yunqi Zhuhong
summary: Late-Ming reviver of monastic discipline at Yunqi si who joined Chan and Pure Land, taught recitation of the name as the principal practice for all, promoted releasing living beings and lay self-examination ledgers, and wrote the Amitābha Sūtra commentary; eighth patriarch in the later Pure Land list; one of the four great masters of the late Ming.

name: Youxi Chuandeng
summary: Ming Tiantai master of Youxi (Tiantai shan) who explained birth in the Pure Land as the birth of non-birth in ten Tiantai gates.

name: Yuan Hongdao
summary: Late-Ming literatus of the Gong'an school who turned from Chan to Pure Land and wrote the Xifang helun.

name: Ouyi Zhixu
summary: Late-Ming master of Tiantai, Vinaya and Pure Land, one of the four great masters, who made faith, vow and practice (holding the name) the three provisions for birth; ninth patriarch in the later list.

name: Xingce
summary: Early-Qing monk who organised seven-day recitation retreats (foqi); tenth patriarch in the later list.

name: Shengan Shixian
summary: Qing monk famed for his Exhortation to Arouse the Mind of Awakening (Quan fa putixin wen), which joins bodhicitta to recitation; eleventh patriarch in the later list.

name: Chewu Jixing
summary: Qing Chan master who turned to Pure Land ('true mind for birth and death, arouse bodhicitta, deep faith and vow, hold the name'); twelfth patriarch in the later list.

name: Yinguang
summary: Modern Chinese master whose letters spread Pure Land practice among lay people: faithfully fulfil one's social duties, avoid evil and do good, believe in cause and effect, and hold the name with faith and vow; established Lingyan shan as a recitation monastery; counted the thirteenth patriarch.

name: Wei Yuan
summary: Qing scholar who compiled the Larger Sūtra into a conflated version and grouped the Samantabhadra chapter with the three Pure Land sūtras as 'four sūtras' (as recalled).
notes: Contribution to the Pure Land canon recalled; low confidence.

name: Kūya
alt_names: Ichi no hijiri 市聖 (saint of the marketplace)
summary: Wandering holy man (hijiri) who recited Amida's name in the streets and markets of Kyoto, dug wells, built bridges and buried the unclaimed dead; the statue at Rokuharamitsu-ji shows six small Amidas issuing from his mouth. Ippen took him as his model ('casting off').

name: Ryōgen
summary: Tendai abbot who restored Mt Hiei, teacher of Genshin; a work on the nine grades of birth is ascribed to him.

name: Genshin
summary: Tendai scholar of Yokawa whose Ōjōyōshū (985) gathered scripture on loathing this defiled world and seeking the Pure Land, on contemplative and oral nenbutsu and on deathbed practice; he organised the Nijūgo zanmai-e, a society of twenty-five monks who vowed to help one another die in right mindfulness. Sixth of the seven Shinshū masters.

name: Yoshishige no Yasutane
summary: Heian literatus, organiser of the Kangaku-e (society joining students and Hiei monks in Lotus lecture and nenbutsu), compiler of the Nihon ōjō gokuraku ki; later took the tonsure as Jakushin.

name: Yōkan
summary: Sanron monk of Tōdaiji lineage and abbot of Zenrin-ji who practised and taught exclusive recitation (Ōjō jūin); tradition says Amida turned to look back at him as he circumambulated (the 'looking-back Amida' of Eikandō).

name: Ryōnin

realization_account.text: In 1117, in samādhi, Amida revealed to him the interfusing nenbutsu (Yūzū nenbutsu engi).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tendai monk of Ōhara, master of shōmyō chant, founder of the Yūzū nenbutsu: he enrolled nobles and commoners — and, in the tradition's account, gods — in a register of nenbutsu practitioners whose recitations interpenetrate.

name: Hōmyō
summary: Monk credited with reviving the Yūzū nenbutsu at Dainenbutsu-ji in the 14th c.

name: Hōnen

realization_account.text: In 1175, reading in Shandao's commentary 'single-heartedly and exclusively recollecting the name of Amida ... this is called the rightly determined act, because it accords with the Buddha's vow', he abandoned other practices; Jōdo-shū holds that he attained nenbutsu samādhi (Sanmai hottokki) and regards him as a manifestation of Seishi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tendai monk who after some thirty years of study found in Shandao the exclusive practice of calling Amida's name, left Mt Hiei and taught it at Yoshimizu to people of every station; wrote the Senchakushū for Kujō Kanezane; was defrocked and exiled in 1207 after the Kōfukuji petition and an incident involving court ladies; returned to Kyoto in 1211 and died in 1212 leaving the One-Sheet Document. Founder of Jōdo-shū and seventh Shinshū master.

name: Eikū
summary: Tendai precept master of Kurodani and Hōnen's teacher, in the lineage of Ryōnin.

name: Kujō Kanezane
summary: Regent and diarist (Gyokuyō) who received precepts from Hōnen and at whose request the Senchakushū was written (1198).

name: Genchi
summary: Hōnen's attendant in his last years, for whom the One-Sheet Document was written; his line (Shirahata/Murasakino) later merged into the Chinzei.

name: Benchō
summary: Hōnen's disciple from Kyushu, founder of the Chinzei line, counted the second patriarch of Jōdo-shū.

name: Ryōchū
summary: Benchō's successor, third patriarch of Jōdo-shū, who spread the Chinzei line in Kamakura and wrote commentaries on Shandao and the Senchakushū.

name: Shōgei
summary: Chinzei scholar who systematised the school's doctrine and its fivefold transmission (gojū sōden).

name: Shōkū
summary: Hōnen's disciple (who helped compile the Senchakushū), founder of the Seizan line.

name: Shōtatsu
summary: Seizan monk of Dazaifu, Ippen's teacher.

name: Kōsai
summary: Hōnen's disciple associated with the 'one-calling' teaching (ichinengi): birth is settled in a single moment of faith, one calling; his line (Ichinen-gi) died out.

name: Ryūkan
summary: Hōnen's disciple associated with the 'many-calling' teaching (tanengi), exiled in the Karoku persecution of 1227; Shinran commended his writings.

name: Chōsai
summary: Hōnen's disciple of the Kuhon-ji line, known for holding that the various practices are also vowed in the primal vow (shogyō hongan gi).

name: Seikaku
summary: Tendai preacher of the Agui line, close to Hōnen, author of the Yuishinshō which Shinran copied and commented on.

name: Kumagai Naozane
summary: Warrior of the Genpei war who became Hōnen's disciple as the monk Rensei; his vow to be born in the highest grade is recorded.

name: Ryōe Dōkō
summary: Jōdo monk who compiled Hōnen's collected words (1274–75).

name: Shunjō
summary: Chion-in abbot to whom the compilation of the 48-scroll illustrated biography of Hōnen is traditionally ascribed.

name: Shinran

realization_account.text: After twenty years as a hall monk on Mt Hiei he secluded himself in the Rokkakudō for a hundred days; on the ninety-fifth dawn Prince Shōtoku (Kannon) appeared in a dream, and he went to Hōnen (Eshinni's letters; Godenshō). He 'abandoned the miscellaneous practices and took refuge in the primal vow' in 1201 (Kyōgyōshinshō postscript).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Hōnen's disciple who, laicised and exiled to Echigo in 1207, called himself 'Gutoku' (foolish bald-head), neither monk nor layman, married Eshinni and taught in the Kantō for some twenty years before returning to Kyoto to write. His Kyōgyōshinshō presents teaching, practice, shinjin and realization as Amida's gift; shinjin is the true cause; the evil person is the true object of the vow. Founder (in the tradition's reckoning) of Jōdo Shinshū; he himself said he had not a single disciple.

name: Eshinni
summary: Shinran's wife, whose letters to their daughter Kakushinni (found in 1921) record Shinran's conversion and her dream of Hōnen as Seishi and Shinran as Kannon.

name: Kakushinni
summary: Shinran's youngest daughter who cared for him in Kyoto and established the Ōtani mausoleum (1272), the origin of the Honganji, as its caretaker.

name: Zenran
summary: Shinran's son, sent to the Kantō, who claimed to have received a secret teaching from his father at night and disparaged the eighteenth vow as a 'withered flower'; Shinran disowned him in 1256 (letters).

name: Yuien
summary: Shinran's disciple of Kawada (Hitachi), generally regarded as the compiler of the Tannishō.

name: Nyoshin
summary: Shinran's grandson (son of Zenran), counted second head of Honganji by Kakunyo's reckoning.

name: Kakunyo
summary: Shinran's great-grandson who made the Ōtani mausoleum into the temple Honganji and claimed for it the orthodox transmission (Shinran–Nyoshin–Kakunyo); author of the Godenshō.

name: Zonkaku
summary: Kakunyo's son and the most learned early Shinshū scholar (Rokuyōshō, the first commentary on the Kyōgyōshinshō); twice disowned by his father.

name: Shinbutsu
summary: Shinran's leading disciple in Takada (Shimotsuke), head of the Takada community from which the Takada branch descends.

name: Jūkaku
summary: Kakunyo's son who compiled Shinran's letters as the Mattōshō (1333).

name: Rennyo
summary: Eighth head of Honganji who, through his letters (Ofumi), congregational meetings (kō) and the practice of enshrining the six-character name, made the small Honganji the largest Buddhist body in Japan; he taught to rely on Amida single-heartedly in the one great matter of the afterlife and to say the nenbutsu in gratitude, while keeping the laws of the land and respecting other deities; revered as the restorer of Shinshū.

name: Kennyo
summary: Eleventh head of Honganji who led the Ishiyama Honganji in its ten-year war against Oda Nobunaga (1570–1580) and surrendered it; his sons Kyōnyo and Junnyo headed the later eastern and western Honganji.

name: Akao no Dōshū
summary: Lay follower of Rennyo from Etchū, remembered as an exemplary myōkōnin for his 'twenty-one resolutions' and austere devotion.

name: Kiyozawa Manshi
summary: Ōtani-ha priest and philosopher who led a reform of the order and taught 'spiritual activism' (seishinshugi), reliance on the Tathāgata as the foundation of the self.

name: Asahara Saichi
summary: Clog-maker of Iwami counted among the myōkōnin, who wrote thousands of verses of the joy and wretchedness of the self embraced by Amida ('Namu Amida Butsu').

name: Ippen

realization_account.text: At the Kumano Hongū in 1274 the deity (as Amida's manifestation) told him that birth had been settled for all by Amida's awakening ten kalpas ago and that he should distribute talismans regardless of faith or purity (Ippen Hijiri-e).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Wandering holy man who gave up home and possessions ('the saint who casts off'), distributed nenbutsu talismans to over 250,000 people and led dancing nenbutsu across Japan; before dying he burned his books, saying all the teachings of his life had become 'Namu Amida Butsu'. Founder of the Ji-shū.
notes: The count of talismans follows the Ippen Hijiri-e as usually reported (moderate).

name: Shinkyō
summary: Ippen's successor who organised the itinerant followers into the Ji-shū order and wrote its regulations.

name: Shōkai
summary: Ippen's disciple (and, by some accounts, younger brother) who compiled the Ippen Hijiri-e (1299).

name: Myōe
summary: Kegon (Huayan) monk of Kōzan-ji, known for strict precepts, dream records and the 'mantra of light'; after reading the Senchakushū he wrote the Zaijarin (1212) charging Hōnen with discarding the aspiration for awakening.

name: Jōkei
summary: Hossō (Faxiang) monk and reformer, devoted to Maitreya, Kannon and Śākyamuni, who drafted the Kōfukuji petition of 1205 against the exclusive nenbutsu.
